headline: Beats 360 Review | Raises the bar for premium lifestyle headphones
body: At ₹42,900, it also shows how the premium headphones category is moving beyond the traditional focus on sound and ANC

Premium headphones have evolved from being primarily about sound to becoming an everyday device that needs to get several things right. Comfort, ANC, call quality, battery life and how well they fit into an active lifestyle now matter just as much. That is also why the premium headphones space has become increasingly competitive, with brands finding different ways to make their products stand out.

The Beats 360 enters this space at ₹42,900, bringing interchangeable earcup and headband cushions, IPX4 resistance and a design aimed at both workouts and everyday use. These additions give the Beats 360 a distinct identity, but the bigger question is how well that approach works in daily use. And with the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Sennheiser HDB 630 also competing in this price range, the Beats 360 has some serious benchmarks to contend with.

So, let’s find out if the Beats 360 has what it takes to stand out.

The biggest change with the Beats 360 is its approach to design. Beats has made the earcups and headband cushions removable, which gives you more flexibility than most premium headphones. You get Performance Knit cushions for workouts and UltraPlush cushions for everyday listening.

I particularly like this idea because it makes sense beyond just customisation. The Performance Knit material is better suited to an active session, while the softer UltraPlush option makes more sense when you are working or travelling. It gives the Beats 360 two personalities without changing the headphones themselves.

The IPX4 rating also adds some much-needed practicality. Sweat and water resistance is still uncommon among premium over-ear headphones. That gives the Beats 360 an advantage if you plan to use them during workouts.

headline: “Phone bombing”: How ‘pranking as a service’ harasses victims
body: Multiple fake messages or calls in under a minute. Victims and abusers of ‘phone bombing’ reveal a freely available tool of digital harassment.

‘Fast and reliable bombing service with unlimited calls and instant delivery,’ says one website that offers ‘pranking as a service’. The site can help mischievous-minded individuals send multiple automated calls to Indian phone numbers.

‘Send up to 1000 calls per hour with speed and anonymity. Perfect for pranking friends or testing systems,’ reads the FAQ section of the website that is easily searchable on Google.

Phone bombing is the practice of putting someone’s phone number on a website, choosing how many fake messages or calls they should receive, and hitting send. This silly act is advertised as “harmless entertainment” and is becoming increasingly common.

The Hindu came upon multiple websites facilitating these phone-bombing prank attacks and spoke to both the victims and abusers of this service.

“It happened to me last year. One of my friends pranked me. They had put my number and the amount of messages on the website. I then received about 50-80 OTP messages,” 20-year-old design student Prashasti (name changed) said.

Her phone was inundated with multiple messages in under a minute while she was in class, attending a lecture. All of them, OTPs, or one-time passwords.

headline: Jay Clayton, Trump’s new AI czar: Who leads the Super Intelligence Force?
body: Trump has been largely favouring light regulation, but the task force reads more like an acknowledgement that some oversight is coming
full_body:

President Donald Trump, on Sunday (October 4, 2026) announced the formation of the Super Intelligence Force (SIF) on Truth Social, shortly after the White House Accord on artificial intelligence , describing the body as tasked with coordinating the federal government’s effort to keep America ahead in a technology that “many say” is bigger than the Industrial Revolution and the Internet.

According to his post, the force will coordinate the government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organisations, critical infrastructure providers and AI companies, and will report to him and Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. Mr. Trump’s statement says the force will be led by four officials: Jay Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence; Andrew Ferguson, Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission; Emil Michael, Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering and Chief Technology Officer; and Scott Kupor, Director of the Office of Personnel Management.

And only one of them is being cast as the face of the effort. Mr. Clayton, per a Wall Street Journal report, will chair the group and effectively be the administration’s AI czar. The White House has not issued a separate press release on that role.

The team has 120 days to report on the risks and opportunities of the technology and on what responsibility the federal government should bear. Other media outlets had noted that Vice-President JD Vance and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth will be members of the AI task force, with David Sacks and Condoleezza Rice advising from outside.

The force’s formation comes against the backdrop of public anxiety over job losses, AI-enabled hacking, weaponisation of the tech and, in the darkest forecasts of some researchers, threats to civilisation. Data centres have also drawn a backlash.

Mr. Trump has been largely favouring light regulation, but the task force reads more like an acknowledgement that some oversight is coming.
